title: Hansel and Gretel
text:
At the edge of a great forest lived a poor woodcutter with his wife and his two children, Hansel and Gretel. When famine came, the wife persuaded her husband to take the children deep into the woods and leave them there, so that there would be fewer mouths to feed.

Hansel overheard. That night he slipped out and filled his pockets with white pebbles, and as they walked into the forest the next day he dropped them along the way. When the children were abandoned, they waited until the moon rose and followed the shining pebbles home. The second time, the door was locked and Hansel could only drop crumbs of bread. The birds ate them, and the children were lost.

After three days they found a little house made of bread with a roof of cake and windows of sugar. An old woman welcomed them in. She was a witch who ate children. She locked Hansel in a stable to fatten him and made Gretel work. When she decided to bake Hansel, she told Gretel to crawl into the oven to test the heat. Gretel said she did not know how; the witch leaned in to show her, and Gretel pushed her in and slammed the door.

Gretel freed her brother. They filled their pockets with the witch's pearls and jewels and found their way home. The wife had died, and their father, who had not had a happy hour since leaving them, wept for joy.
lesson: Siblings who keep their heads and look out for each other can get through what neither could manage alone.
people: Hansel, Gretel, their father, their mother (later stepmother), the witch
source: Brothers Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmarchen, No. 15 (Hansel und Gretel)
caveat: In the 1812 first edition the woman is the children's own mother; the Grimms made her a stepmother in later editions.
